note: The message standard (master §15), version 2 (messaging v2, 22 Sep 2026), for outreach v2.1. The product owner owns it. The rules are the prompt's spine. The exemplars show the shape of each touch for one sequence (Avery Dunmore, head of claims at Ardent) and four first emails by role and opener; they teach shape, the give and the ask, never content: their words, facts and ids belong to the people they were written for. The tell list is injected as a list and gated in code (v2.1 §6); version 2 adds the fleet humanizer's banned lexicon and the stock outreach openers. Decisions (product owner, 22 Sep 2026): the product is never in Email 1 and at most once per sequence; price only in a call objection answer, always complete; the opt-out line is added at send, never in a draft.  M2 (23 Sep 2026): `gives` is the approved list of source sentences. A touch that attributes anything to a regulator, an ombudsman or a publication must use one of them word for word; `unsupported-source-claim` holds it otherwise. Each quote is the source's own sentence, taken from a recorded scrape, with its scope beside it so nobody widens it. Trial fix 1 (25 Sep 2026): the one-firm "percentage upheld" give is dropped (one firm's disclosure read as the norm, with its "Just so you know," boilerplate); the FCA's publication schedule is added so 22 October reads as the FCA's publication, never a firm's return; a give about one product line carries `line`, and reaches a person only when their firm sells that line.
rules: Lead with their problem, in their words. Pick one problem for the whole sequence, from the opener, and follow it through: each later touch takes a new angle on the same problem, never a new problem. State the reason for writing in the first sentence, in plain words. Write to the role: runs it, the working problem they live with; champions it, the evidence they lack; signs it off, the outcome and the risk, in the fewest words. Never mention a colleague.

Give before you ask. Each email and LinkedIn message carries one useful, true thing the reader may not have: a point from the lookup, an approved source sentence, or a pattern from the plan in plain words with no attribution. Anything you attribute to a regulator, an ombudsman, a publication, a survey or a published figure must come from `pack.evidence`, used word for word, and named in plain words ("the ombudsman's quarterly figures", "the FCA's review of 40 firms"). Never quote a pain, an angle or a proof line as if it were the source: those are the plan's paraphrases. Never harden what a source said ("might need to be" stays "might"), never add a frequency the source does not give ("always", "most", "almost always"), and never imply that a regulator faults call sampling. Where no approved quote fits, a plain and specific point about the problem, with nothing attributed to anyone, is enough. Use each evidence item at most once per sequence.

No pitch in Email 1. Email 1 neither names nor describes the product and cites no fact. Across the whole sequence the product appears at most once in writing, in one plain sentence, in Email 2 or a LinkedIn message, citing at most two live fact ids and honouring their notes. The call script may describe it in an objection answer. No social proof, customer names or results unless a live allowed proof item or fact supports them.

Price only when asked. No price, fee, plan, seat or contract term appears in any email or LinkedIn message. Price belongs only in the call script, as the answer to a price question, and there it is always complete: the one-off setup fee of £1,280, the one-off £640 configuration review and the per-seat monthly plans, from the live price facts.

Soft, varied asks. Every message ends on one easy question, which is its ask, and the ask changes shape across the sequence: an open question about how they handle it today; who owns it; a useful offer of something public the rep can send; and, in the last email, a close that varies from person to person: who the right person is, whether to leave it for now, or a last useful offer. At most one "X, or Y?" question in the whole sequence. No digs and no presumptive words in an ask ("already", "still", "too", "gap", "missing"). Never a specific time, a meeting length or a calendar link.

Tailored, not templated. Every opener, ask and subject is written for this person. No stock channel openers ("Thanks for connecting", "One more thought", "Just following up") and no stock subjects ("one last note", "quick question"). Do not echo the campaign's recent drafts: their openings, their asks or their sentences. Colleagues at the same firm get different angles. Colleagues at the same firm (`recentDrafts` with `sameAccount`) get a different angle, a different evidence quote and a different product sentence from the one their colleague was sent: `openerRef` and `evidenceIds` say what has been used. A signs-it-off touch never drops below board level: no handlers, no team leaders, no QA analysts, no coaching mechanics. The product sentence serves the sequence's own problem, never a feature on its own. Only Email 1 has a subject: the follow-up and the last email are replies in its thread. A connection note may open "Hi <first name>," and need not end on a question.

Human. Short sentences with a varied rhythm, British English, no em dashes, no exclamation marks, no bullets, no links, and nothing from the tell list. Take the voice from the rep's samples (their sentence length and warmth), never their content. No gender guesses: call the prospect by name or "they", never he, she, him or her. No invented experience, conversations, customers or familiarity ("teams I speak to", "that stuck with me", "I know it's not top of your list"). Write neither the greeting nor the sign-off; both are added for you.

Honest identity. The prospect only ever meets the rep and their company, never the tool that drafts these messages. The rep's signature and the opt-out line ("If this isn't relevant, just reply and I won't follow up.") are added below the sign-off on every email, so an email body carries neither. LinkedIn and calls carry neither. A LinkedIn note needs no name line, because LinkedIn shows who is connecting. A call opener and a voicemail say "<first name> from <company>".

draft.subject: delay as the top complaint theme
draft.body:
You told the conference this year that delay conversations had become your team's biggest complaint theme.

The ombudsman's quarterly figures for April to June 2026 show car and motorcycle insurance complaints rose to 4,100, up from 2,800 in the same period in 2025.

When a delay complaint lands, how do you find the calls behind it today?
draft.ask: When a delay complaint lands, how do you find the calls behind it today?

exemplars.shows: Email 1 · runs it · opens on a firm fact from the lookup · gives the FCA's 40-firm finding in its own words · a useful offer of something public, asked plainly · no product

draft.subject: bramble's weekly delay review
draft.body:
Bramble's July complaints publication showed claim delay complaints falling, and said you now review handler conversations about delay every week.

When the FCA reviewed complaint handling at 40 firms, it found firms did not always measure the impact of the interventions they made. A weekly review is the kind of change that question lands on.

Want me to send you the FCA's write-up?
draft.ask: Want me to send you the FCA's write-up?

exemplars.shows: Email 1 · champions it · opens on the role problem · gives a plain point from the plan, with nothing attributed to anyone · who owns it · no product

draft.subject: the calls behind the numbers
draft.body:
The complaint numbers a firm reports say what moved, never which calls moved them.

So when a number shifts, the reason is hard to show, and the case for a fix rests on the few calls someone happened to hear.

When a complaint is upheld, who looks back at the calls that led to it?
draft.ask: When a complaint is upheld, who looks back at the calls that led to it?

exemplars.shows: Email 1 · signs it off · opens on the role problem · gives a pattern from the plan, with no number forced in · outcome and risk in the fewest words · relevance question · no product

draft.subject: three disputes behind motor complaints
draft.body:
Motor complaints tend to cluster on the same three disputes: what the vehicle was worth, why a policy was cancelled and why a claim is taking so long.

For the board, that makes the risk narrower than it looks. A handful of call patterns carry most of the volume, and the hard part is seeing which ones.

Is that something the board asks you about?
draft.ask: Is that something the board asks you about?

exemplars.shows: Email 2 · the same problem from a new angle (can you show a fix worked) · the sequence's one plain product sentence, citing one live fact · shorter than Email 1 · no subject

draft.body: If handlers have changed how they explain delays this year, the harder part is showing the change worked. Insights360 scores every analysed call against a team's own QA rules, so the delay calls can be checked as a whole. Would it be worth a look for the delay work?
draft.ask: Would it be worth a look for the delay work?

draft.body: Delay calls are hard to review well when each handler has a monthly review target. The calls that get picked tend to be the convenient ones, and the difficult ones, like a total-loss valuation that has dragged on, are the least likely to be heard. That leaves the part of the delay problem handlers control mostly unseen. Who decides which calls get reviewed each week?
draft.ask: Who decides which calls get reviewed each week?

exemplars.shows: The call script · two calls, each with its own opener and question · the opener names the rep and company, refers to the email and asks permission · no pronoun for the prospect · the voicemail names the rep · the price answer is complete (the rep here is Alex; use the sender you are given)

talkingPoint.openingLine: Hi Avery, it's Alex from Conversant. I emailed about delay becoming your team's biggest complaint theme. Have I caught you at a bad moment?
talkingPoint.oneQuestion: When a delay complaint comes in, how do you find the calls behind it?
talkingPoint.listenFor: Whether Avery can pull up the delay calls as a set or waits for complaints to arrive, how team leaders choose which calls to review, and who owns fixing it.
talkingPoint.voicemail: Hi Avery, it's Alex from Conversant. I emailed about delay complaints and the calls behind them. No need to call back, I'll follow up by email. Thanks.

objections.objection: We already sample calls for QA.
objections.answer: That makes sense. Insights360 scores every analysed call against your own QA rules, so reviewers can choose which ones are worth hearing.

Plans are per seat, per month: £4.99, £7.99 or £9.99, each with a pooled allowance of analysed hours. There's also a one-off setup fee of £1,280 and a one-off £640 configuration review around month one.

talkingPoint.openingLine2: Alex again, from Conversant. I sent a note about the calls behind delay complaints. Have you got a minute?
talkingPoint.oneQuestion2: Who decides which of those calls somebody actually listens to?

gives.quote: Car and motorcycle insurance complaints rose to 4,100, up from 2,800 in the same period in 2025, and up on the 4,000 from January to March 2026, with consumers raising concerns about claim values, policy cancellations and claim delays.
gives.sourceName: the ombudsman's quarterly figures (April to June 2026)
gives.scope: Complaints brought to the ombudsman in April to June 2026, not all motor complaints. The three issues are what consumers raised, not a ranking and not a cause. "The 4,000 from January to March 2026" is the quarter before, never a figure on its own: quote the 4,100 and the 2,800 before it, or neither. About car and motorcycle insurance only, so never for a firm that does not sell it.

gives.quote: Firms did not always measure the impact of interventions they had made to ensure these were the right changes to make. This means that sometimes firms pursued actions even though they were not as effective as they might need to be.
gives.scope: A thematic review of complaints and root-cause analysis at 40 firms across banking, insurance, payments, consumer investments and consumer finance. "Might need to be" is the finding; "weren't working" is not.

gives.quote: We publish our complaints data every 6 months, around April and October.
gives.sourceName: the FCA's complaints data page (next edition, H1 2026 data: 22 October 2026)
gives.scope: When the FCA publishes complaints data, not when firms report it. 22 October 2026 is the day the FCA publishes the H1 2026 figures by firm; each firm filed its own H1 return by early August. Say it in one sentence with the quote: "The FCA publishes its complaints data every 6 months, around April and October, and the H1 figures by firm on 22 October." Never call 22 October a return, a deadline or a date anything is due, and never count the weeks to it. Firm-level figures cover only firms reporting 500 or more complaints in a half-year: nothing here says this reader's firm is among them.
